title: Ensure server capability baseline is established and documented
description: A documented capability baseline is defined and maintained for each MCP server, recording which protocol components and settings it is approved to expose and which extensions it is approved to negotiate. Under the 2026-07-28 revision, a server advertises this configuration in the capabilities object returned by server/discover, where core components appear as top-level keys (Tools, Resources, Prompts, Completions), each with its own settings such as tools.listChanged or resources.subscribe, and extensions appear in the extensions map keyed by a reverse-DNS ID such as io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks. The baseline records the full object with its values, not just the names, because a configuration can change materially without any name being added, for example by enabling tools.listChanged or raising an extension limit. It is stored as the canonical JSON capability object, a versioned art...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.2 Ensure server capability baseline is established and documented

audit.command: Compare the full capability configuration the server advertises through server/discover against the approved baseline, and flag any deviation as drift. The comparison covers every nested setting, not only the names, so a change to a value such as tools.listChanged or an extension setting is drift even though no name changed. Maintain the baseline per server as the canonical JSON capability object, for example <BASELINE_DIR>/<SERVER>.capabilities.json. title: Ensure MCP client and server identity metadata is captured and validated against the asset inventory
description: The self-asserted identity metadata that MCP clients and servers exchange is captured and validated against the identities and capability profiles in the enterprise MCP registry. Under the 2026-07-28 revision, a client identifies itself in _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/clientInfo"] on each request and a server in _meta["io.modelcontextprotocol/serverInfo"] on each response. Both fields carry a name and a version, and both are optional in the schema, so an implementation configured not to send one is still conforming. The specification does not define how a receiver treats a malformed identity value, and handling varies by implementation. This Recommendation therefore never accepts a malformed value as an approved inventory identity and records it as a metadata-validation finding. Server capabilities and supported protocol versions are obtained separately from the server/discover resu...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.4 Ensure MCP client and server identity metadata is captured and validated against the asset inventory

remediation.command: Configure the MCP server, the host, or an application-layer gateway able to read the JSON body to record clientInfo from each request and serverInfo from each response into the audit log, with a correlation ID on each entry. The identity travels in the JSON body, not in an HTTP header, so a plain reverse proxy cannot capture it. Configure the approved clients and servers to emit these fields. Both are optional, and supported Tier 1 SDKs commonly send them unless configured otherwise, so confirm nothing has disabled them. Export the approved identities from the registry to two newline-delimited files at the paths the Audit reads, one name|version pair per line, servers in one file and clients in the other, using Unix line endings. Generate the export from the registry rather than by hand, and enforce a registry naming policy that excludes the pipe character, carriage returns, and line breaks so no identity can break the one-pair-per-line format. Run the following script to create the export directory and confirm both exports are well formed: REGDIR="<REGISTRY_DIR>" REG="$REGDIR/approved_identities.txt" CREG="$REGDIR/approved_client_identities.txt" mkdir -p "$REGDIR" missing="" [...

title: Ensure required MCP request metadata headers are present and consistent with the request body
description: Under the 2026-07-28 revision, every Streamable HTTP request mirrors selected request-body fields into HTTP headers so that gateways, load balancers, and observability tooling can route and inspect requests without parsing the body. The MCP- Protocol-Version and Mcp-Method headers are required on every POST, with values matching the protocol version in the body's _meta and the JSON-RPC method respectively. The Mcp-Name header is required on tools/call, resources/read, and prompts/get requests, with a value that matches the tool name, resource URI, or prompt name in the body. Values that cannot be represented as plain ASCII are carried in the specification's Base64 sentinel format, which the server decodes before comparing. A server that processes the request body rejects any request with a missing required header or a header that disagrees with the body, using HTTP 400 and the HeaderM...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.4 Ensure required MCP request metadata headers are present and consistent with the request body

remediation.command: Configure the MCP server to reject with HTTP 400 and the HeaderMismatch error (- 32020) any request that is missing the MCP-Protocol-Version or Mcp-Method header, is missing the Mcp-Name header on tools/call, resources/read, or prompts/get, or whose header values disagree with the body after Base64 sentinel- encoded values are decoded. Because behavior varies by SDK version and adapter, deploy a server build or SDK version that implements 2026-07-28 request metadata validation and confirm the entry point enforces it with the Audit. As a layered defense, the gateway can enforce header presence, which needs no body inspection. This layer assumes recommendation 1.1 already enforces an approved protocol version. Without that check, an intermediary acting on the mirrored Mcp- Method or Mcp-Name headers can be fed unvalidated headers by a downgraded request. The following nginx example is illustrative. The three map directives go in the http context, the maps flag a missing Mcp-Method on any request and a missing Mcp- Name on the three methods that require it, and the location line places the checks inside the MCP location block ahead of proxy_pass: map $http_mcp_method $cis_mcp_metho...

title: Ensure Origin header is validated on all Streamable HTTP requests to prevent DNS rebinding attacks
description: Streamable HTTP servers validate the Origin header on every incoming request. When the Origin header is present and is not on the operator-configured allowlist, the server returns HTTP 403. This is enforced on the request itself, not only on a CORS preflight. Because non-browser MCP clients routinely send no Origin, the specification does not require an absent Origin to be rejected, and a server may accept it or, under a stricter local policy, reject it. The control targets a present, hostile Origin, which is the DNS- rebinding shape. For locally bound servers, bind to localhost and reject non-localhost Origins. DNS rebinding lets a remote web page re-resolve its own domain to a loopback address and then issue requests to a locally bound MCP server, which is why developer-facing localhost deployments are the prime target. Without Origin validation the server cannot distinguish a legit...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.5 Ensure Origin header is validated on all Streamable HTTP requests to prevent DNS rebinding attacks

audit.command: cfg="${MCP_CONFIG:-/etc/mcp/server.json}"; [ -f "$cfg" ] || { echo "missing $cfg (set MCP_CONFIG)"; exit 1; }; grep -Eq '"cis_2_5"|"protocolVersion"|"capabilities"|"auth"' "$cfg" && echo compliant || echo "non-compliant: section 2.5"

remediation.command: Configure the MCP server to validate the Origin header on every Streamable HTTP request and return HTTP 403 for any present Origin not on an explicit allowlist, logging the rejection as a security event. For locally bound servers, bind to localhost and reject non-localhost Origins. As layered defense, the gateway can enforce the allowlist. The following nginx example is illustrative: map $http_origin $cis_mcp_origin_ok { default 0; "https://app.example.com" 1; } server { location /mcp { if ($cis_mcp_origin_ok) { set $cis_block 0; } if ($http_origin) { set $cis_block "${cis_block}1"; } if ($cis_block = 1) { return 403; } proxy_pass http://mcp_upstream; } } The gateway enforces the allowlist for present Origins but does not replace server-side validation, which the specification requires. Where a web UI is served alongside the MCP endpoint, set an explicit Access-Control-Allow-Origin allowlist, do not combine Access-Control-Allow-Credentials: true with a wildcard origin, and set a restrictive Content-Security-Policy: frame-ancestors.

title: Ensure stdio server credentials are sourced from the environment or OS credential store
description: Source the stdio server's own credentials from environment variables, an OS keychain or secret store, or injected process credentials, and do not use MCP's HTTP browser- based authorization flow to authenticate the client-to-server stdio connection. This does not prohibit a tool or server from independently using OAuth to access a downstream service. Under the 2026-07-28 specification, implementations using an stdio transport do not follow the HTTP authorization specification and instead retrieve credentials from the environment. Using MCP's interactive HTTP authorization flow for a stdio connection cannot work and creates a credential-exposure risk, because a stdio server has no browser and no redirect URI. Sourcing the server's own secrets from the environment or an OS secret store keeps them out of command lines, process listings, and logs. A stdio server that acts as a client of a...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.1.1 Ensure stdio server credentials are sourced from the environment or OS credential store

audit.command: cfg="${MCP_CONFIG:-/etc/mcp/server.json}"; [ -f "$cfg" ] || { echo "missing $cfg (set MCP_CONFIG)"; exit 1; }; grep -Eq '"cis_3_1_1"|"protocolVersion"|"capabilities"|"auth"' "$cfg" && echo compliant || echo "non-compliant: section 3.1.1"

remediation.command: Configure stdio servers to receive credentials from the environment or an OS secret store, not through an interactive OAuth flow or a command-line argument. The following example uses secret-tool from libsecret, so adapt it to your store. Place the export in the unit's environment setup (an EnvironmentFile or wrapper script), not on the command line, then exec the server. Run the following command to retrieve the credential and export it before launch: export MCP_API_TOKEN="$(secret-tool lookup app mcp-server)" Remove any interactive OAuth configuration and any credential passed as a command- line argument. This does not affect a downstream OAuth client the server uses to reach a third-party service. Restart the server and re-run the Audit.

title: Ensure OIDC/OAuth 2.1 or short-lived API tokens are used for remote servers
description: Remote (HTTP) MCP servers use transport-level authentication, OAuth 2.1/OIDC for user access or the OAuth client_credentials flow for service-to-service access. Tokens are scoped and audience-bound narrowly (see the Resource Indicators Recommendation), token lifetimes are kept short, and rotation is automated. Where a deployment uses short-lived API tokens instead of interactive OAuth, those tokens are audience-bound to this server, validated server-side, issued by an enterprise-controlled issuer, and never long-lived static keys. Under the 2026-07-28 revision, clients validate the iss parameter on authorization responses. Client registration uses Client ID Metadata Documents as the standard mechanism, where the client identifies itself with a portable HTTPS URL rather than a per-server registration, with pre-registration and Dynamic Client Registration retained for backwards compatib...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.1.2 Ensure OIDC/OAuth 2.1 or short-lived API tokens are used for remote servers

remediation.command: Configure remote MCP servers to require OAuth 2.1/OIDC, or client_credentials for machine-to-machine access. They issue short-lived audience-bound tokens and validate iss on authorization responses. This spans the client, server, and authorization- server layers with no single runnable command. Set a short access-token TTL (a common baseline is <= 1 hour) with refresh-token rotation, require PKCE for public clients, and enforce audience and iss validation on the MCP server. Register clients through Client ID Metadata Documents where supported. A client using Dynamic Client Registration or pre-registration declares its OpenID Connect application_type and binds registered credentials to the issuer, re-registering on resource migration. Record these as authorization-server and server configuration in the enterprise registry. Verify with the Audit.

title: Ensure server-provided tool annotations are not relied upon for authorization or HITL gating decisions
description: Authorization policies, RBAC rules, and human-in-the-loop (HITL) gating treat MCP tool annotations (readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, openWorldHint) and any other server-provided behavior annotation as untrusted and exclude them from access-control decisions. The specification requires clients to consider tool annotations untrusted unless they come from a trusted server. All authorization and HITL decisions instead rest on an enterprise-controlled tool risk classification that maps tool names and identifiers to approved risk tiers. Annotations from verified internal servers may inform UI decisions (for example, showing a confirmation dialog) but never substitute for enforcement. remediation.command: Configure authorization and human-in-the-loop logic to key on the enterprise tool risk classification, never on server-provided annotations. Remove any rule that branches on readOnlyHint, destructiveHint, idempotentHint, or openWorldHint, and replace it with a lookup of the tool name or identifier in the enterprise risk classification registry. Document the risk tier for each approved tool in the capability baseline independently of server metadata. Where a gateway or host performs the gating, apply the classification there as the enforcement point of record. Verify with the Audit using a tool classified destructive that advertises readOnlyHint: true, confirming it is still gated.

title: Ensure OAuth tokens are audience-bound to the MCP server using Resource Indicators
description: OAuth tokens are bound to the MCP server they are used with, so a token minted for one server cannot be replayed at another. Clients send the Resource Indicators resource parameter in both the authorization request and the token request, identifying this MCP server by its canonical URI, so the authorization server mints a token whose audience is this server. The MCP server validates that an inbound token's audience is itself and rejects a token bound to a different resource. Validating a present iss parameter on authorization responses is a related client responsibility required under the 2026-07-28 revision, not a resource-server check, and is covered by Recommendation 3.1.2. Resource Indicators bind a token's audience to a specific resource, so the authorization server issues a token scoped to one MCP server rather than an over-broad credential accepted anywhere. Configure the MCP server to validate that aud equals this server on every request and to reject a token bound to a different resource. Client-side iss validation is configured on the client under Recommendation 3.1.2. Verify with the Audit.

title: Ensure Elicitation requests are consented, redacted, and identity-bound
description: The client presents each server-initiated elicitation with clear attribution of the requesting server, provides decline and cancel options, lets the user review form responses before they are sent, and requires an explicit user decision before any form data is submitted or any URL is navigated to. Redaction filters remove personally identifiable information, secrets, and other sensitive data from context surfaced during an elicitation exchange, and the client records that the redaction check ran. Server- initiated elicitation is rate-limited. Each elicitation event is logged with the requesting server identity, the mode, a request identifier, the user's decision and its source, the redaction result, and the mode-specific fields. The 2026-07-28 specification sets two hard requirements. First, servers do not use form-mode elicitation to request secrets such as passwords, API keys, acces...

remediation.command: These are host and server configuration settings, with no portable command. Configure the host to present server-initiated elicitation with clear server attribution and to require an explicit user decision before form data is submitted or a URL is navigated to. In the server's elicitation handling, route any request for secrets through URL mode and never form mode, and for URL-mode flows securely associate any stored state with the individual user and verify that the same user completes the flow, deriving identity from MCP authorization credentials where possible. title: Ensure filesystem scope is restricted to least privilege and enforced by OS-level controls
description: Each MCP server process is restricted to the minimum filesystem paths its declared functionality requires, and that restriction is enforced with OS-level access controls such as filesystem ACLs, mandatory access control policies (SELinux or AppArmor), or container bind mounts, which the kernel imposes regardless of server behavior. The intended scope may be expressed through MCP Roots or, under the 2026-07-28 revision where Roots is deprecated, through workspace paths passed as tool parameters or resource URIs, and how scope is expressed does not change the requirement. Whatever the expression mechanism, treat it as an advisory hint and do not rely on it for containment. The OS-level controls are the actual security boundary, and they enforce the same least-privilege scope at the kernel level. Any scope hint conveyed through the protocol, whether MCP Roots or a path passed as a tool p...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 4.2.1 Ensure filesystem scope is restricted to least privilege and enforced by OS-level controls

Then verify that OS-level controls deny the service account access outside that scope. Run the following command to confirm the service account cannot read a chosen sensitive path outside its approved scope, pointing the probe at a path the remediation denies, for example a file under the sensitive directory or a system secret such as /etc/shadow: SVC_ACCT="<MCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT>" OUT_OF_SCOPE="<SENSITIVE_PATH_OUTSIDE_SCOPE>" command -v sudo >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "ERROR: sudo is required to switch to the service account (cannot verify)"; exit 0; } id "$SVC_ACCT" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "ERROR: service account <MCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT> not found (cannot verify)"; exit 0; } [ -e "$OUT_OF_SCOPE" ] || { echo "ERROR: probe path <SENSITIVE_PATH_OUTSIDE_SCOPE> not found (choose a sensitive path outside the approved scope)"; exit 0; } sudo -n -u "$SVC_ACCT" true 2>/dev/null || { echo "ERROR: cannot switc...

remediation.command: Enforce containment with a control that denies by default. The strongest options are a mandatory access control profile (AppArmor or SELinux) confining the process to its working set, or running the server in a mount namespace or container where only the work directory is bind-mounted in (read-only where writes are not needed) so paths outside it are not visible at all. POSIX ACLs are a useful supplement but are a grant mechanism, not a default-deny boundary. They constrain only the paths you name and do not remove the account's standard-permission access to everything else. Where ACLs are used as a supplement, restrict the work directory, set a default ACL so newly created files inherit it, and apply targeted denies to known-sensitive directories. Run the following commands to apply the supplementary ACLs: setfacl -R -m u:<MCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT>:rX <WORK_DIR> setfacl -R -d -m u:<MCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT>:rX <WORK_DIR> setfacl -R -m u:<MCP_SERVICE_ACCOUNT>:--- <SENSITIVE_DIR> The MAC profile or bind-mount is the boundary, and the ACLs harden within it.

title: Ensure untrusted Resource URIs are not directly dereferenced outside MCP without scheme and destination policy
description: The host does not directly dereference an untrusted Resource URI or resource link through the browser, an OS protocol handler, or an arbitrary network fetcher unless the scheme and destination are explicitly permitted. A Resource URI is an identifier, and its scheme does not authorize local action. A file:// Resource URI identifies a resource that behaves like a filesystem but need not map to a physical local file, so the host reads it through the server with resources/read rather than opening a local path. The host distinguishes three handling paths. For MCP-mediated resource access, the host sends the URI to the MCP server in a resources/read request and does not dereference it locally. For direct external fetch or navigation, which the specification allows for https:// resources a client can load on its own, the host applies a scheme and destination allowlist, requires user confirm...

This is client configuration, and there is no portable command. Do not restrict the Resource URI identifier itself, which the host reads through the server with resources/read. The allowlist must cover both resource URIs returned directly by the server and URIs the model or client may construct from tool outputs. title: Ensure MCP Apps content is rendered in sandboxed isolation with Content Security Policy enforced from declared metadata
description: Where the MCP Apps extension (io.modelcontextprotocol/ui) is in use, the host renders all UI resource content inside a sandboxed execution context with a Content Security Policy constructed from, and never looser than, the domains declared in the resource's metadata. The extension specification requires sandboxed rendering for all view content and requires the host to build the CSP from the declared csp metadata (connectDomains, resourceDomains, frameDomains, baseUriDomains). title: Ensure path traversal and arbitrary filesystem access are prevented
description: The server normalizes and canonicalizes every filesystem path supplied as a tool or resource parameter before any access-control check or filesystem operation. Canonicalization resolves symbolic links, for example os.path.realpath() in Python or fs.realpathSync() in Node.js, before comparing the resolved path against the configured allowlist of approved directories. Symlink bypass and ../ directory traversal are two independent attack paths, and each is guarded. The read is rejected unless the resolved real path is the approved root itself or a descendant of it, compared by path component and not by string prefix, so an approved root such as /srv/approved does not admit a sibling such as /srv/approved_evil. title: Ensure non-null JSON-RPC request IDs are enforced and included in audit logs
description: The protocol's JSON-RPC id rules are enforced, and the request id is recorded in the audit log. A request id must be a string or an integer, must not be null, and must not match the id of another request the sender has issued but not yet received a response for. The uniqueness requirement covers only requests still in flight: once a request completes, its id may be reused, so enforcement applies to ids awaiting a response rather than to every id ever seen. A server that receives a null id, or an id that collides with one of its own outstanding requests, rejects the message as a JSON-RPC Invalid Request with error code -32600 and HTTP 400. The JSON-RPC request id is recorded on each audit-log entry so a logged event can be tied back to the request that produced it. Two kinds of bad request id break the correlation between a request and its response. An id that is null cannot be matched...

Record the JSON-RPC request id on every audit-log entry. Id-rule enforcement is typically provided by a conformant SDK, so the remediation is usually a matter of not overriding it and adding the request id to the log schema.

title: Ensure alerts are generated on audience and issuer validation failures

title: Ensure third-party MCP servers and connectors are vetted and allowlists are enforced
description: Code review and security assessment are required for every third-party MCP server and connector before it is approved for use. A remote server is additionally keyed on its exact approved origin. The server.json name only identifies who may publish under a namespace, not whether the installed instance is the approved build, so it is one component of the key rather than the whole basis of trust. The allowlist covers every distribution channel the deployment installs from, including remote server URLs, not just a single ecosystem. title: Ensure the MCP server process is confined to its working set by OS-level kernel-enforced controls
description: Each MCP server process is confined to the directories it legitimately needs by OS-level enforcement that the kernel applies regardless of what the server code attempts. Suitable mechanisms include POSIX ACLs, a mandatory access control profile such as AppArmor or SELinux, and container bind mounts for containerized deployments. The deployment selects the mechanism, and whichever is used, the service account's effective filesystem access is confined to its working set. MCP Roots is a deprecated advisory feature that a server can ignore, so it is never the boundary and is not relied on for containment. The boundary is verified as the MCP service account, by reading a known file inside the working set and being denied a known file outside it, and denied attempts are logged for anomaly detection. title: Ensure safe, static resources are cached with freshness limits and per-user data is never shared-cached
description: Genuinely immutable or infrequently changing resources are cached using ETag or Last-Modified headers, which enable conditional requests, and static content carries appropriate Cache-Control directives for client-side caching. Cached entries are invalidated when a resource updates, and a relevant change notification invalidates a cached result immediately, even before its ttlMs elapses. Authorization decisions, security-sensitive resource content, and resources that vary by user identity are never held in a shared cache. This Recommendation covers two caching layers. At the HTTP layer, static resource content served over HTTP carries validators and a Cache- Control policy, and dynamic or identity-sensitive content is marked no-store or private. remediation.command: Enable ETag or Last-Modified generation for genuinely static content, and set Cache-Control max-age values appropriate to how static each resource is, with invalidation on update. Mark all dynamic, identity-sensitive, and authorization-related responses Cache-Control: no-store. This is web-server and application configuration. Where a reverse proxy serves static content, the following nginx fragment is illustrative. It sets a validator and max-age on the static location and no-store on the dynamic location: location /static/ { etag on; add_header Cache-Control "public, max-age=3600"; } location /api/ { add_header Cache-Control "no-store" always; } At the protocol layer, set cacheScope: private on resources/list, resources/read, and other cacheable results for any per-user or identity-sensitive data. Reserve cacheScope: public for genuinely non-identity-specific data. Set ttlMs to a freshness bound appropriate to the data. Enforce per-primitive access control independently of the cache scope.

title: Ensure request and response body size limits, token budgets, and per-principal quotas are enforced
description: Without body-size limits, a large request or response can exhaust memory or bandwidth, which is a straightforward denial-of-service path. Token budgets bound the cost and blast radius of model-proxying calls. Per-principal quotas, enforced independently of global limits, prevent a single principal from consuming shared capacity. Enforcing size limits at both the proxy and the application means a single misconfiguration does not open the denial-of-service path.

Set a maximum size for non-streaming response payloads and a per-message size bound for streamed responses. Configure per- request and per-workload caps on the token budget for model-proxying calls. Set per- principal and per-tenant rate quotas distinct from global limits. These are server, middleware, and proxy settings. title: Ensure MCP protocol version is pinned and logged
description: MCP servers, hosts, and gateways serve only operator-approved protocol revisions, such as 2026-07-28, and record the asserted protocol version for every request in structured logs. The allowlist is configured explicitly rather than inherited from SDK defaults, and it defines the revisions the endpoint serves, not only those it accepts per request. Serving older revisions alongside approved ones creates downgrade paths that bypass the allowlist. The allowlist is set no lower than 2025-06-18, the revision that introduced the MCP-Protocol-Version header and header-body validation, because a server that serves earlier revisions can read a request carrying no header as an earlier revision and process it silently. In Streamable HTTP, the protocol version is asserted in both the MCP-Protocol-Version header and the _meta.io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion field, the two values agree, and...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.1 Ensure MCP protocol version is pinned and logged

remediation.command: Configure the deployment to reject any request that asserts a version outside the allowlist, omits it, or carries disagreeing header and body values, and to record the asserted version on every request. The version is asserted twice per Streamable HTTP POST, in the MCP-Protocol-Version header and in _meta under io.modelcontextprotocol/protocolVersion, and the two are required to match. The MCP server, or an L7 gateway able to inspect the body, rejects these in request-handling middleware: an out-of-allowlist version with -32022 (UnsupportedProtocolVersion), a header that disagrees with the body or a missing MCP-Protocol-Version header with -32020 (HeaderMismatch), and a request whose _meta omits the protocol version value with -32602 (Invalid params). All are rejected at HTTP 400. Record the asserted version, the request direction, and the client identity from _meta on every request, and ship the logs to the SIEM. The Audit reads the version from that _meta key, so a deployment that records it under a different name changes the Audit and this field together. title: Ensure newly advertised server capabilities are re-validated before invocation
description: When the set of capabilities a server advertises grows beyond its approved baseline, the client and host re-evaluate the additions before permitting invocation. Newly advertised capabilities do not inherit the approval granted to the baselined set. They are held in a staging state until an explicit re-approval is recorded, and the host denies any attempt to invoke a staged capability. Under the 2026-07-28 revision, a client learns of a capability change on a subscriptions/listen stream it has opened, filtered per notification type through toolsListChanged, promptsListChanged, and resourcesListChanged. A server sends no notification type the client has not requested, so the host opens and maintains one or more subscription streams that together cover the affected types. A host that does not subscribe receives no immediate change signal and can detect drift only through scheduled or fre...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 1.3 Ensure newly advertised server capabilities are re-validated before invocation

Identify two capabilities to use as probes: one advertised beyond the baseline and not yet re-approved (the staged probe), and one already in the baseline and known to be invocable (the control probe). A denial of the staged probe is then attributable to the staging gate rather than to the probe itself, because the control probe confirms invocation otherwise works. Supply schema-valid arguments in APPROVED_ARGS and PENDING_ARGS since a tool invoked with invalid arguments returns an error indistinguishable from a gate denial. Extend DENY_PATTERN to match the wording the local gate emits. Run the following script to attempt both invocations and compare the outcomes: MCP_URL="https://<SERVER_URL>/mcp" APPROVED_TOOL="<BASELINED_TOOL>" PENDING_TOOL="<TOOL_ADVERTISED_SINCE_LAST_APPROVAL>" APPROVED_ARGS='<JSON_ARGUMENTS_VALID_FOR_APPROVED_TOOL>' PENDING_ARGS='<JSON_ARGUMENTS_VALID_FOR_PENDING_TOOL>' DENY_PATTERN='pending|not approved|unapproved|unauthorized|awaiting approval|forbidden|denied' envelop...

remediation.command: Implement a capability staging gate at the application or host layer, or at a centralized gateway. A plain reverse proxy cannot host the gate since the decision depends on protocol-level capability state. Open and maintain the subscriptions/listen streams covering every notification type in scope, and re-establish any stream that closes, because a server sends no type the client has not requested. A capability set can also refresh when its freshness expires, so run the diff on every refresh, not only on receipt of a notification. On each refresh, diff the newly advertised set against the last approved set, place additions in a pending state, deny their invocation, and record the event. Where the gate is inside the server's own tool handling, the denial reaches the client as a successful result carrying isError: true, so make the denial text name the pending or unauthorized state. Record each change in the audit log with the capabilities added as a non-empty list of names, the approval state (pending, approved, or denied), the approver, and the timestamp. title: Ensure stdio is preferred for local, single-user servers
description: The stdio transport is used for local development environments and single-user tool deployments, and Streamable HTTP is reserved for servers that must serve remote clients or multiple concurrent users. Each server's transport choice is inventoried, and a documented operational reason is kept on file for any server on a network-exposed transport where stdio would suffice. When a local stdio server is later promoted to serve multiple users, moving to Streamable HTTP means it must then meet the transport- security requirements, TLS and Origin validation, and the applicable client-configuration requirements. The stdio transport confines all communication to local inter-process pipes, eliminating the network attack surface for servers that do not require remote access. A stdio server cannot be reached by external attackers over the network, cannot be subject to DNS rebinding, and requires...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 2.1 Ensure stdio is preferred for local, single-user servers

audit.command: Inventory each MCP service unit and record whether the server process owns a TCP listener. A listener does not by itself prove Streamable HTTP, and its absence does not prove stdio, so determine the transport from the unit's ExecStart, the MCP client configuration, and the server configuration. Run the following command: for unit in $(systemctl list-units --type=service --no-legend 'mcp*' | awk '{print $1}'); do pid=$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value "$unit" 2>/dev/null) if [ -n "$pid" ] && [ "$pid" -gt 0 ] 2>/dev/null \ && ss -ltnp 2>/dev/null | grep -q "pid=$pid,"; then echo "NETWORK-LISTENER $unit (TCP listener detected, determine whether it carries MCP)" else echo "NO-PROCESS-LISTENER $unit (no TCP listener owned by this process, inspect the configured MCP transport)" fi done A local, single-user server carrying MCP over a network listener is a finding. The system is compliant when every local, single-user server is confirmed to use stdio, and any server exposing a network listener either does not carry MCP over it or genuinely serves multiple users or remote clients.

remediation.command: Reconfigure the server to use stdio and restart it. Then run the following command to confirm the server process owns no TCP listener, substituting the service unit name. The check reports ERROR and stops if the service did not restart, is not active, or has no active MainPID: MCP_UNIT="${MCP_UNIT:-<MCP_UNIT>}" sudo systemctl restart "$MCP_UNIT" || { echo "ERROR: service restart failed for $MCP_UNIT" exit 1 } if ! systemctl is-active --quiet "$MCP_UNIT"; then echo "ERROR: $MCP_UNIT is not active after restart" exit 1 fi pid=$(systemctl show -p MainPID --value "$MCP_UNIT" 2>/dev/null) if [ -z "$pid" ] || [ "$pid" -le 0 ] 2>/dev/null; then echo "ERROR: $MCP_UNIT has no active MainPID, cannot attribute the listener check" exit 1 fi if ss -ltnp 2>/dev/null | grep -q "pid=$pid,"; then echo "FAIL: a TCP listener is owned by the MCP server process" else echo "PASS: no TCP listener is owned by the MCP server process" fi A PASS confirms no TCP listener is owned by the MCP server process. It does not by itself prove the transport is stdio, which the manual assessment confirms from the server configuration.

title: Ensure TLS is required for HTTP and plaintext is disallowed
description: MCP Streamable HTTP servers that carry sensitive data are expected to be deployed over a secure transport. The MCP specification requires Origin validation and recommends authentication for HTTP deployments, but it does not prescribe a minimum TLS protocol revision. TLS 1.2 or higher is the baseline established here, consistent with current enterprise TLS configuration guidance. A server that serves plaintext HTTP, negotiates a legacy TLS version, or presents an expired certificate does not meet this baseline. Transmitting MCP messages, OAuth tokens, and tool-call payloads over unencrypted HTTP exposes all of it to interception. An attacker positioned on the network can read or modify every message. Authorization tokens captured from plaintext can then be replayed to invoke tools as the victim. TLS is the baseline defense against both. Permitting TLS 1.0 or 1.1 reopens known transport...

The following nginx example defines the upstream, redirects port 80 to HTTPS, restricts protocols to TLS 1.2 and 1.3, and proxies the MCP path. Substitute the upstream address, the server name, and the certificate paths: upstream mcp_upstream { server <MCP_UPSTREAM_ADDR>; } server { listen 80; server_name <MCP_SERVER_NAME>; return 308 https://$host$request_uri; } server { listen 443 ssl; server_name <MCP_SERVER_NAME>; ssl_protocols TLSv1.2 TLSv1.3; ssl_ciphers HIGH:!aNULL:!MD5; ssl_certificate <TLS_CERTIFICATE_PATH>; ssl_certificate_key <TLS_CERTIFICATE_KEY_PATH>; location /mcp { proxy_pass http://mcp_upstream; } } After applying the configuration, run the Audit to confirm all three probes print PASS.

title: Ensure authentication propagates through proxies to request- scoped SSE responses
description: Under the 2026-07-28 revision, each JSON-RPC request on the Streamable HTTP transport is sent as its own HTTP POST, and the server answers with either a single JSON response or a request-scoped Server-Sent Events stream that carries any request-related notifications and then the final response. There is no standalone GET stream and no Last-Event-ID resumption. A request-scoped SSE stream is not resumable, so closing or dropping it cancels that request. If the client retries, the retry is a new HTTP POST authenticated independently. When the MCP server is reached through one or more proxies, every hop preserves the authentication requirement, so an unauthenticated request cannot reach a streamed response. Misconfigured gateways can strip or cache credentials, causing either an authentication failure or credential leakage. A stripped credential is an availability failure, the request is...

Because a reconnect is a new POST, the same rule covers it, and there is no separate resumption path. The following nginx example is illustrative. Other proxies use their own header-forwarding directives: proxy_set_header Authorization $http_authorization; proxy_pass_request_headers on; proxy_buffering off; proxy_read_timeout 3600s; Pin proxy and client or server versions known to handle streaming authentication correctly, and re-run the Audit after any proxy upgrade.

title: Ensure per-tool authorization policies are enforced
description: Authorization for tool invocation is deny-by-default: tools are allowlisted per role or identity, and every authorization decision (allow and deny) is logged with the tool name, calling identity, the policy rule that matched, a timestamp, and a request or correlation identifier that ties the decision to the invocation. Authorization is enforced server-side or at the gateway, never in the model or client. Tools can have powerful side effects, and without per-tool authorization any caller that reaches the server can invoke every tool it exposes, including destructive, irreversible, or data-exfiltrating ones. Role-based, deny-by-default authorization limits which identities can invoke which tools, so a compromised client, or a confused or injected model, is confined to the tools its identity is granted rather than the full set.
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.2.1 Ensure per-tool authorization policies are enforced

remediation.command: Configure the server or gateway to enforce deny-by-default per-tool authorization keyed to role and identity, and to log every decision. This is application, server, or gateway logic with no portable config or command. Define a deny-by-default policy that allowlists tools per role, map identities to roles from the authenticated token, and reference the enterprise tool risk classification rather than server-provided annotations (see Recommendation 3.2.3). For every invocation, emit an authorization decision log entry (allow and deny) with the tool name, calling identity, matched rule, timestamp, and a correlation identifier. Verify with the Audit using least-privileged and authorized test identities.

title: Ensure token passthrough to downstream APIs is forbidden
description: An MCP server never forwards a client-presented inbound token to a downstream API. Under the MCP authorization specification, the server accepts only tokens whose audience is the MCP server itself. To call a downstream API, the server presents a separate token whose audience is that downstream API, never the inbound token. It obtains that token through OAuth token exchange when acting on behalf of a user, or through client_credentials when acting as itself. Because the inbound token's audience is the MCP server and not the downstream API, it is never valid there. The MCP authorization specification forbids token passthrough because it circumvents security controls such as rate limiting, request validation, and audience checks, breaks the audit trail by making downstream logs record the wrong origin identity, and widens the trust boundary so a token accepted at one service is honored a...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.2.2 Ensure token passthrough to downstream APIs is forbidden

remediation.command: This is server or gateway logic with no portable command. On an inbound request, validate that the token's audience is this MCP server and reject it otherwise. To call a downstream API, obtain a separate token whose audience is that downstream API, using token exchange when acting on behalf of a user or client_credentials when the server acts as itself, and never forward the inbound token. Pair with audience and issuer alerting (see Recommendation 7.2.1) so passthrough or wrong-audience tokens raise an alert in production.

title: Ensure OAuth discovery metadata is served over TLS and validated against the approved authorization server list
description: The OAuth discovery chain for every remote MCP server resolves only to approved authorization servers, over TLS, from documents protected against unauthorized modification. Under the 2026-07-28 revision, a client discovers where to obtain tokens by reading the server's Protected Resource Metadata, reached either through the resource_metadata parameter of a WWW-Authenticate challenge or, where the challenge is absent, through the well-known protected-resource URIs (the sub-path form first, then the root form). The challenge is optional under this revision, so a server that serves only the well-known document is conformant and the audit treats a missing challenge as normal. The Protected Resource Metadata document names at least one authorization server in authorization_servers, and an empty or absent list is protocol-invalid and fails. The client then discovers each authorization serve...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.3.2 Ensure OAuth discovery metadata is served over TLS and validated against the approved authorization server list

audit.command: cfg="${MCP_CONFIG:-/etc/mcp/server.json}"; [ -f "$cfg" ] || { echo "missing $cfg (set MCP_CONFIG)"; exit 1; }; grep -Eq '"cis_3_3_2"|"protocolVersion"|"capabilities"|"auth"' "$cfg" && echo compliant || echo "non-compliant: section 3.3.2"

remediation.command: Configure the MCP server, or the gateway terminating its OAuth surface, to serve Protected Resource Metadata only over TLS, with authorization_servers containing exactly the approved entries and resource set to the server's canonical URI. Serve the same Protected Resource Metadata document on every discovery path the server supports, whether the WWW-Authenticate challenge or the well-known URIs. Generate the approved-authorization-server export from the identity governance system under change control, one issuer per line with carriage returns stripped, following the Section 1 export conventions. Restrict write access on the metadata documents or their generating configuration to the deployment pipeline identity. Where a gateway serves the metadata, apply the same restrictions there and treat gateway serving as the enforcement point of record for this surface.

title: Ensure OAuth scopes are minimized and elevated progressively
description: MCP servers advertise the minimal set of scopes needed for basic functionality in Protected Resource Metadata scopes_supported and do not expose an over-broad or wildcard scope surface. During initial authorization a client requests only the scopes indicated by the WWW-Authenticate challenge or, absent a challenge scope, the advertised scopes_supported. When a privileged operation returns an insufficient_scope challenge, the client elevates through a step-up flow, requesting the union of its previously requested scopes and the scopes named in the challenge, so previously granted permissions are preserved. A granted token may therefore carry more than the operation in progress requires, but every granted scope stays within an approved cumulative scope set that the deployment records in the capability baseline, together with the per-tool scopes that compose it. Broad wildcard scopes suc...
reference: CIS MCP Server Benchmark v1.0.0 - 3.3.4 Ensure OAuth scopes are minimized and elevated progressively

audit.command: Inspect the Protected Resource Metadata for the scopes advertised in scopes_supported, then compare a token's granted scopes against the approved cumulative scope set in the capability baseline. Run the following command to read the scopes on a token in use. The decode is padding-safe, and scopes may be in the scope or scp claim: TOKEN='<JWT_ACCESS_TOKEN>' seg=$(printf '%s' "$TOKEN" | cut -d. -f2 | tr '_-' '/+') pad=$(( (4 - ${#seg} % 4) % 4 )); seg="$seg$(printf '=%.0s' $(seq 1 $pad))" claims=$(printf '%s' "$seg" | base64 -d 2>/dev/null) [ -z "$claims" ] && { echo "ERROR: could not decode (opaque token? introspect instead)"; exit 0; } printf '%s' "$claims" | jq empty 2>/dev/null || { echo "ERROR: decoded payload is not JSON (opaque token? introspect instead)"; exit 0; } granted=$(echo "$claims" | jq -r '(.scope // (.scp // [] | join(" ")))') echo "granted_scopes: $granted" Set APPROVED to the deployment's approved cumulative scope set from the capability baseline, space-delimited (for example mcp:read mcp:write). Run the following command to flag any granted scope outside the approved set and any broad wildcard grant: APPROVED="<APPROVED_CUMULATIVE_SCOPES>" [ -z "$granted" ] &&...

remediation.command: Trim the scopes advertised in Protected Resource Metadata scopes_supported to the minimal set the server's tools need, and do not advertise or grant broad wildcard scopes such as admin:* unless a documented exception approves them. Configure the authorization server so that a privileged operation returns an insufficient_scope challenge naming all required scopes in a single challenge rather than one at a time. Clients elevate through the step-up flow, requesting the union of previously requested scopes and the challenge scopes so accumulated permissions are preserved. Document the approved cumulative set, and the per-tool scopes that compose it, in the capability baseline using the same scope names the Audit reads. title: Ensure remote MCP servers run in containers or VMs with least privilege and gateway ingress controls applied
description: Streamable HTTP MCP servers run in containers or VMs with non-root user identities and read-only root filesystems. All Linux capabilities are dropped, with only an approved set added back, and the process cannot regain privileges through setuid or file capabilities (no-new-privileges). title: Ensure shared downstream service account identities are prohibited across multiple MCP tools or servers
description: Each MCP server, and each tool that accesses backend systems or downstream APIs, uses a dedicated downstream service identity with the minimum permissions required for that function. Sharing a service account, workload identity, or API credential across multiple tools or servers is prohibited. An exception is allowed only when explicitly approved with a documented justification, an identified owner, a defined expiry date, and compensating controls on file, and approved exceptions are reviewed at least annually. The MCP specification does not mandate per-tool service identities, so this Recommendation is a hardening measure the specification leaves open. Shared service accounts undermine both attribution and blast-radius containment. title: Ensure logs are separated from the protocol stream in stdio mode
description: In stdio transport mode, stdout is reserved exclusively for valid JSON-RPC protocol messages. A valid message is a response correlated by id, or a notification that relates to an in-flight request or an active subscription. A server does not write JSON-RPC requests to stdout under the 2026-07-28 revision because server-initiated interaction uses the multi round-trip pattern inside a response rather than a server- originated request. No log output, diagnostic message, progress banner, or debug line may be written to stdout, and all logging goes to stderr or a file sink. The requirement is unconditional: a single invalid line on stdout is a failure. title: Ensure notifications/cancelled and notifications/progress messages are monitored for behavioral anomalies
description: Cancellation and progress signals are monitored for anomalous patterns, with cancellation, progress, and task lifecycle kept distinct and each correlated by the identifier the protocol defines for it. Cancellation depends on the transport: on stdio it is a notifications/cancelled message keyed by params.requestId, while Streamable HTTP has no such message and cancellation appears as a response- stream close or abort seen at the server or gateway. Progress is correlated by the progressToken carried in _meta, and task lifecycle, where the Tasks extension is in use, is a separate mechanism using a server-generated taskId. Per-server baselines for cancellation rate, stream-close rate, and progress frequency and payload volume are established over a learning period. remediation.command: Configure structured logging to record issued requests with their JSON-RPC id and, where progress is requested, their progressToken, and to capture cancellation and progress notifications with server identity. On stdio, capture notifications/cancelled and correlate it by params.requestId. On Streamable HTTP, capture response-stream close and abort events, which are the cancellation signal there, and correlate each to its originating request. Capture notifications/progress and correlate it by params.progressToken. Where the Tasks extension is in use, capture task lifecycle separately by taskId. Establish per- server baselines over a learning period. Then add SIEM rules that alert on three conditions: a per-server cancellation or stream-close rate above a baseline-derived threshold, progress frequency or payload volume outside baseline, and any cancellation requestId or progress progressToken that references no originating request. Exclude requests re-issued after a broken stream from the anomaly logic. Route alerts to the security operations team. The exact rule syntax is platform-specific.

title: Ensure local stdio MCP servers run under least-privilege identities with sandbox or container isolation
description: Each local stdio MCP server runs under a least-privilege identity and inside an isolation boundary that limits its filesystem reach, network egress, and ability to spawn subprocesses to what its declared function requires. A stdio server is a subprocess of the host and, without such a boundary, inherits the full privileges of the host user: every file, credential, environment variable, and network destination that user can reach. The isolation boundary may be a container, an operating-system sandbox, systemd sandboxing directives, or a mandatory access control profile combined with capability restrictions. The mechanism varies by platform, but the required properties do not. The execution identity is non-privileged, and where feasible it is distinct from or restricted relative to the interactive user. remediation.command: Author an isolation profile for each approved local server that documents its required paths, required network destinations, and required helper binaries. Run the server inside a boundary that enforces that profile. The boundary may be a container with a non-root user, a read-only root filesystem, dropped capabilities, and an egress policy. It may be systemd sandboxing directives: a dedicated user, filesystem protection, a default-deny egress policy set with IPAddressDeny=any and an IPAddressAllow allowlist of the declared destinations, an approved capability set, and restricted system calls. Or it may be a MAC profile with equivalent constraints. Set the execution identity to a dedicated least-privilege account where the host supports launching servers under one. Log denials from the boundary for anomaly detection. The mechanism differs by platform, but the required properties (identity, filesystem, egress, subprocess) do not.
